words.intro: Cologne station is the busiest junction in the west. You have four minutes to change. The train you need left before you arrived, or will leave after you’ve gone. Either way, there is an announcement.

grammar[0].fact: Trains in Germany are punctual less often than the country’s reputation suggests: in some recent years only about two out of three long-distance trains were on time. Swiss railways have been known to stop late German trains at the border rather than let them disturb their timetable.

document.intro: A real form, filled in by hand, from a real late train. We have cut out the English half and the small print. You only need the first few lines and the boxes with handwriting.
document.fact: You can now fill this form in online or in the DB app, but paper is still accepted.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Find it in the handwriting and write it.
reading.intro: Max must be in Cologne for a wedding, and he has a four-minute change. His report to Deutsche Bahn begins in a sober, written way. He has to fill in a form for his money back, and he has decided to be thorough. The form has one line for “Reason”.
reading.fact: In the EU a passenger gets 25 per cent of the fare back if the train is an hour late, and half if it’s two hours or more. The German form is called the *Fahrgastrechte-Formular*, and you can pick it up at any Reisezentrum. It’s the most-read document in German rail.
reading.tasks[1].instruction: Complete with hatte, war or the past form, as in the text.
